claim: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins contain sequence-distributed molecular features that are conserved over evolution, despite little sequence similarity that can be detected in alignments.
source: In previous work, we showed that intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins contain sequence-distributed molecular features that are conserved over evolution, despite little sequence similarity that can be detected in alignments (Zarin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Zarin et al., 2019).

claim: Elevated isoelectric point and hydrophobicity are positively associated with mitochondrial localization.
source: We experimentally confirm that elevated isoelectric point and hydrophobicity, features that are positively associated with mitochondrial localization, are necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the Cox15 mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Elevated isoelectric point and hydrophobicity are necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
source: We experimentally confirm that elevated isoelectric point and hydrophobicity, features that are positively associated with mitochondrial localization, are necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis experiments showing loss of mitochondrial localization when these features are reduced.

claim: Increasing isoelectric point in a synthetic IDR restores weak mitochondrial targeting.
source: Remarkably, increasing isoelectric point in a synthetic IDR restores weak mitochondrial targeting.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations increasing pI in a simulated IDR partially restore mitochondrial localization.

claim: IDRs play key roles in diverse aspects of cell biology.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are increasingly appreciated as playing key roles in diverse aspects of cell biology (Forman-Kay and Mittag, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Bioinformatics methods identify thousands of IDRs in eukaryotic proteomes.
source: Bioinformatics methods identify thousands of IDRs in eukaryotic proteomes (Dosztányi et al., 2005; Uversky, 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published bioinformatics methods.

claim: For the vast majority of IDRs, it is currently difficult to obtain high-specificity predictions of biological function.
source: for the vast majority of IDRs, it is currently difficult to obtain high-specificity predictions of biological function or to identify which amino acid residues within them are important for function (van der Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article discussing the challenges in IDR function prediction.

claim: For folded regions, similarity to homologous protein sequences offers highly specific and diverse predictions of biological function.
source: For folded regions, similarity to homologous protein sequences offers highly specific and diverse predictions of biological function (El-Gebali et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a database/resource describing domain-based function prediction.

claim: IDRs often show little sequence similarity detectable in alignments.
source: However, IDRs often show little sequence similarity detectable in alignments
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about IDR sequence properties and is contrasted with folded regions.

claim: Despite little conservation in amino acid sequence alignments, IDRs contain sequence-distributed molecular features that are likely under natural selection and associated with biological function.
source: Recent studies indicate that despite little conservation in amino acid sequence alignments, IDRs contain sequence-distributed molecular features, such as biophysical properties, repeats, and short linear motifs, that are likely under natural selection and associated with biological function (Zarin et al., 2019; Zarin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FAIDR can predict diverse functions for IDRs based on their amino acid sequences.
source: Here we describe a first general approach to predict diverse functions for IDRs and to identify molecular features that are important for those functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript, including cross-validation performance data.

claim: FAIDR can identify molecular features that are important for IDR functions.
source: Here we describe a first general approach to predict diverse functions for IDRs and to identify molecular features that are important for those functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of molecular features associated with various functions shown in Figure 3 and experimental validation in Figure 4.

claim: FAIDR identifies molecular features associated with functions such as subcellular organization and signaling.
source: Using this approach, we identify molecular features that are associated with functions such as subcellular organization and signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis and feature identification shown in Figure 3.

claim: FAIDR can predict a role in transcription for the N-terminal IDR in uncharacterized yeast protein Mfg1.
source: We also demonstrate how our approach can predict a role in transcription for the N-terminal IDR in an uncharacterized yeast protein Mfg1, based in part on evolutionary variation in polyglutamine repeats.
evidence: The claim is supported by FAIDR predictions shown in Figure 5 and inference based on molecular features.

claim: The prediction of transcription function for Mfg1 is based in part on evolutionary variation in polyglutamine repeats.
source: We also demonstrate how our approach can predict a role in transcription for the N-terminal IDR in an uncharacterized yeast protein Mfg1, based in part on evolutionary variation in polyglutamine repeats.
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 5C, which highlights the variance in glutamine content.

claim: FAIDR uses an expectation-maximization (E-M) algorithm to infer hidden variables.
source: To ensure that the model infers only a few important molecular features for each function, we use LASSO regularization (Hastie et al., 2015) and to infer the hidden variables, we use an expectation–maximization (E–M) algorithm (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: FAIDR uses LASSO regularization to ensure that the model infers only a few important molecular features for each function.
source: To ensure that the model infers only a few important molecular features for each function, we use LASSO regularization (Hastie et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim describes the computational method used in the study, with a citation to the statistical method.

claim: FAIDR automatically determines which IDRs are likely to be responsible for each function.
source: The model automatically determines which IDRs are likely to be responsible for each function and which features are most informative for each function (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim describes a capability of the FAIDR model as implemented and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: FAIDR automatically determines which features are most informative for each function.
source: The model automatically determines which IDRs are likely to be responsible for each function and which features are most informative for each function (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim describes a capability of the FAIDR model as demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Evolutionary signatures are vectors of Z-scores that summarize the deviations of 82 molecular features in disordered regions from the distribution of those features obtained from simulations of IDR evolution.
source: As previously described (Zarin et al., 2019), to summarize the molecular features of IDRs, we used evolutionary signatures, vectors of Z-scores that summarize the deviations of 82 molecular features in disordered regions from the distribution of those features obtained from simulations of IDR evolution.
evidence: The claim describes the computational method used, with citation to previous work.

claim: For each molecular feature in evolutionary signatures, the mean and (log) variance are calculated across a set of orthologous IDRs, leading to a total of 164 features.
source: For each molecular feature, we calculate the mean and (log) variance across a set of orthologous IDRs, which leads to a total of 164 features describing the evolution of these molecular features in each IDR.
evidence: The claim describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: FAIDR trained on evolutionary signatures performs as well or better than state-of-the-art predictors of mitochondrial targeting signals (Mitofates).
source: We find that the held-out predictions from FAIDR do as well or better than state-of-the-art predictors of mitochondrial targeting signals and Cdc28 substrates that were specifically designed to predict these functions (Mitofates and Condens, respectively) (Fukasawa et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2012; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve comparisons shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FAIDR trained on evolutionary signatures performs as well or better than state-of-the-art predictors of Cdc28 substrates (Condens).
source: We find that the held-out predictions from FAIDR do as well or better than state-of-the-art predictors of mitochondrial targeting signals and Cdc28 substrates that were specifically designed to predict these functions (Mitofates and Condens, respectively) (Fukasawa et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2012; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve comparisons shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A diverse set of protein annotations and phenotypes can be predicted with reasonable power using FAIDR (overall average fivefold cross-validation AUC = 0.81).
source: We found a diverse set of protein annotations and phenotypes that could be predicted with reasonable power (overall average fivefold cross-validation AUC = 0.81, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, gray bars)
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Predictable functions using FAIDR range from well-characterized IDR functions such as signal transduction and mitochondrial targeting, to underappreciated IDR functions such as ribosome biogenesis and DNA damage.
source: ranging from well-characterized IDR functions such as signal transduction and mitochondrial targeting, to underappreciated IDR functions such as ribosome biogenesis and DNA damage
evidence: The claim is supported by the list of predictable functions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: FAIDR can predict function from single-species profiles of molecular features (82 sequence features computed from Saccharomyces cerevisiae IDR sequences alone).
source: Indeed, we found that the 82 sequence features (Zarin et al., 2019) computed from Saccharomyces cerevisiae IDR sequences alone (scaled to unit variance and 0 mean) could also predict protein function (overall average fivefold cross-validation AUC = 0.77, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, unfilled bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The predictive power of single-species features is significantly less than evolutionary signatures (paired t-test over 23 classes p<0.001).
source: Although the overall power was significantly less than the evolutionary signatures (paired t-test over 23 classes p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of the two approaches.

claim: Related functions group together in hierarchical clustering analysis of molecular features.
source: Encouragingly, we found that related functions group together in this analysis (Figure 3A, indicated by symbols above function names).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Proteinaceous membraneless organelles (PMLOs) cluster with several phenotypes and functions related to RNA.
source: For example, consistent with their putative functions (Darling et al., 2018), proteinaceous membraneless organelles (PMLOs) (Figure 3A, unfilled square) clustered with several phenotypes and functions related to RNA (Figure 3A, filled square).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Signaling-associated functions such as Cdc28 kinase substrates, signal transduction, and protein kinase activity share an increase in KEN degradation boxes.
source: For example, signaling-associated functions such as Cdc28 kinase substrates, signal transduction, and protein kinase activity share an increase in KEN degradation boxes (Figure 3B,i)
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cdc28 substrates are distinguished by increased CKS1 docking sites and CDK consensus sites.
source: while Cdc28 substrates (as expected) are distinguished by increased CKS1 docking sites and CDK consensus sites (Figure 3B,i).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with expected biology.

claim: DNA damage response is associated with the presence of PCNA/Pip boxes, Mec1/Tel1 consensus sites, and NLSs (nuclear localization signals).
source: The DNA damage response seems to share some features with the more general functions discussed above, but is also (as expected) associated with the presence of specific motifs: PCNA/Pip boxes, Mec1/Tel1 consensus sites (Lai et al., 2012), and NLSs (nuclear localization signals) (Figure 3A,ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Signal transduction and protein kinase activity share increased histidine residues.
source: Signal transduction and protein kinase activity share increased histidine residues (Figure 3B,i), which we speculate is related to histidine kinase signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Increased histidine residues in signal transduction and protein kinase activity may be related to histidine kinase signaling.
source: Signal transduction and protein kinase activity share increased histidine residues (Figure 3B,i), which we speculate is related to histidine kinase signaling.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: A decrease in histidine residues is predictive of essentiality ('inviable' phenotype) and nuclear pore localization.
source: Interestingly, the opposite (a decrease in histidine residues) is predictive of essentiality ('inviable' phenotype) and nuclear pore localization (Figure 3A,iii).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The presence of PRK1 consensus sites is a predictor of actin cortical patch function.
source: Other features that are consistent with known disordered region function include the presence of PRK1 consensus sites as a predictor of actin cortical patch function (Figure 3A,iv) (Sekiya-Kawasaki et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Increased isoelectric point is a predictor of mitochondrial functions.
source: and increased isoelectric point as a predictor of mitochondrial functions (Figure 3A,v) (reviewed in Jaussi, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The presence of RGG and K/A/P repeats are among the strongest predictors for all PMLOs.
source: As expected, we found the presence of RGG (Chong et al., 2018) and K/A/P repeats (van der Lee et al., 2014) among the strongest predictors for all these compartments (Figure 3B,vi).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: A decrease in threonine residues is associated with PMLOs and all RNA-related functions.
source: We also found a decrease in threonine residues associated with these, as well as all the RNA-related functions (Figure 3B,viii), which to our knowledge has not been previously reported.
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B and is stated as a novel finding.

claim: Stress granules are distinct from all other bodies, showing a decrease in the variance of basic residues and lysine repeats.
source: We found that stress granules are distinct from all other bodies, showing a decrease in the variance of basic residues and lysine repeats (Figure 3B,vii).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nucleoli and associated ribosomal functions show increased CKII consensus sites.
source: Nucleoli and associated ribosomal functions are distinct in that they show increased CKII consensus sites (Figure 3B,vi).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Processing body (P body) proteins show an increased variance in Mec1 consensus sites.
source: We also found that processing body (P body) proteins show an increased variance in Mec1 consensus sites, while mRNPs and mRNA binding proteins show a decrease in this feature (Figure 3B,ix).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: mRNPs and mRNA binding proteins show a decrease in variance of Mec1 consensus sites.
source: We also found that processing body (P body) proteins show an increased variance in Mec1 consensus sites, while mRNPs and mRNA binding proteins show a decrease in this feature (Figure 3B,ix).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminal IDR of Cox15 protein is a known mitochondrial targeting signal.
source: For this, we chose the N-terminal IDR of the Cox15 protein, which is a known mitochondrial targeting signal (Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a proteomics study.

claim: Mean isoelectric point is the top predictive molecular feature for Cox15 IDR 1 association with mitochondrial localization.
source: The top predictive molecular feature (a positive predictor) is mean isoelectric point (pI), which also has a relatively high Z-score in the Cox15 IDR 1 feature vector.
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Increased hydrophobicity is a top positive predictor present in the Cox15 IDR.
source: Another top positive predictor that is present in this IDR is increased hydrophobicity (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutating each arginine residue (R) in the wild-type Cox15 IDR to glutamic acid (E) lowers the pI from 12.40 to 4.04.
source: We first created a mutant IDR with lower pI by mutating each arginine residue (R) in the wild-type IDR sequence to a glutamic acid (E), which lowered the pI of the wild-type IDR from 12.40 to 4.04 while only minimally changing the hydrophobicity (Figure 4B, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental design and sequence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The wild-type GFP-tagged Cox15 strain has a clear mitochondrial localization.
source: As expected, the wild-type GFP-tagged Cox15 strain has a clear mitochondrial localization (Figure 4C, left; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'Cox15 IDR low pI' strain no longer localizes to the mitochondria.
source: However, the 'Cox15 IDR low pI' strain no longer localizes to the mitochondria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated pI is necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
source: This provides evidence that the elevated pI is necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental result showing loss of mitochondrial localization when pI is reduced.

claim: The 'Cox15 IDR low hydrophobicity' strain fails to localize to the mitochondria.
source: Interestingly, the 'Cox15 IDR low hydrophobicity' strain also fails to localize to the mitochondria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated hydrophobicity is necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
source: which indicates that elevated hydrophobicity is also necessary for mitochondrial targeting function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental result showing loss of mitochondrial localization when hydrophobicity is reduced.

claim: The strain in which the N-terminal IDR of GFP-tagged Cox15 is replaced with a simulated IDR fails to show a mitochondrial localization pattern.
source: Nevertheless, consistent with the functional importance of the sequence-distributed features, the strain in which the N-terminal IDR of GFP-tagged Cox15 is replaced with this simulated IDR fails to show a mitochondrial localization pattern (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first few conserved amino acids in the Cox15 IDR, the predicted cleavage site and helicity are not sufficient for mitochondrial localization.
source: indicating that the first few conserved amino acids in the IDR, the predicted cleavage site and helicity (Figure 4B) are not sufficient for mitochondrial localization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental result showing that a simulated IDR preserving these features does not localize to mitochondria.

claim: Increasing the pI of the simulated Cox15 IDR from 10.2 to 12.2 partially rescues mitochondrial localization.
source: Remarkably, this mitochondrial localization phenotype seems to be partially rescued when the pI of the simulated IDR is increased ('sim IDR high pI', Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated pI in the context of a synthetic, non-functional Cox15 N-terminal disordered region is sufficient to restore weak mitochondrial targeting function.
source: This indicates that the elevated pI in the context of a synthetic, non-functional Cox15 N-terminal disordered region is sufficient to restore weak mitochondrial targeting function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental result showing partial rescue of mitochondrial localization when pI is increased in the simulated IDR.

claim: Functional associations with evolutionary signatures revealed by the FAIDR statistical model can be used to design mutations in IDRs that alter phenotype in predictable ways.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that functional associations with evolutionary signatures revealed by the FAIDR statistical model can be used to design mutations in IDRs that alter phenotype in predictable ways
evidence: The claim is supported by the Cox15 mutagenesis experiments demonstrating predictable changes in mitochondrial localization.

claim: A small number of molecular features may be necessary and sufficient for partially restoring some IDR functions.
source: and suggest that a small number of molecular features may be necessary and sufficient for partially restoring some IDR functions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that modulating pI and hydrophobicity affects mitochondrial targeting.

claim: There are currently 739 uncharacterized ORFs in the yeast proteome.
source: There are currently 739 uncharacterized ORFs in the yeast proteome, of which 121 have one or more IDRs for which we are able to make predictions.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD).

claim: 121 uncharacterized ORFs in the yeast proteome have one or more IDRs for which FAIDR can make predictions.
source: There are currently 739 uncharacterized ORFs in the yeast proteome, of which 121 have one or more IDRs for which we are able to make predictions.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the yeast proteome using FAIDR.

claim: The N-terminal IDR in putative mitochondrial protein SHH3 is predicted to be associated with the mitochondrion and the mitochondrial inner membrane.
source: One interesting example is the N-terminal IDR in putative mitochondrial protein SHH3, which we predict to be associated with the mitochondrion, as well as the mitochondrial inner membrane.
evidence: The claim is based on FAIDR predictions for an uncharacterized protein.

claim: SHH3 assumes a mitochondrial localization in the LoQAtE database and Yeast RGB.
source: Indeed, SHH3 assumes what looks to be a mitochondrial localization in recent localization collections such as the LoQAtE (Localization and Quantitation Atlas of the yeast proteomE) database (Breker et al., 2014; Breker et al., 2013) and Yeast RGB (Dubreuil et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to localization databases.

claim: FAIDR predicts that an IDR in MFG1 is associated with sequence-specific DNA binding.
source: Another interesting case is an IDR in MFG1, which FAIDR predicts to be associated with sequence-specific DNA binding (Figure 5A), indicating that MFG1 could be a transcription factor.
evidence: The claim is based on FAIDR predictions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All other IDRs with a higher probability for association with transcription factor activity according to FAIDR are IDRs from confirmed transcription factors (Sok2, Sfp1, Mot3).
source: Indeed, all other IDRs with a higher probability for association with transcription factor activity according to FAIDR are IDRs from confirmed transcription factors (Sok2, Sfp1, Mot3) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FAIDR predictions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mfg1 regulates filamentous growth by interacting with the FLO11 promoter and regulating FLO11 expression.
source: Despite being an uncharacterized ORF, Mfg1 regulates filamentous growth by interacting with the FLO11 promoter and regulating FLO11 expression (Ryan et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Mfg1 has a nuclear localization.
source: and has a nuclear localization (Huh et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a localization study.

claim: Increased variance of glutamine residues in Mfg1 is a positive predictor of its association with transcription factor activity.
source: For example, increased variance of glutamine residues in Mfg1 is a positive predictor of its association with transcription factor activity (Figure 5C, orange box)
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FAIDR stands in contrast with methods established for specific subtypes of IDRs and existing methods that use amino acid sequences to predict whole-protein function.
source: Our method stands in contrast with those established for specific subtypes of IDRs, as well as existing methods that use amino acid sequences to predict whole-protein function.
evidence: The claim is a statement about how FAIDR differs from other approaches.

claim: The goal of FAIDR is to generate hypotheses about both the function of individual IDRs and which molecular features in those IDRs are important for those functions.
source: Our goal is to generate hypotheses about both the function of individual IDRs and which molecular features in those IDRs are important for those functions, much like Pfam annotations provide both predictions of molecular functions of domains and hypotheses about specific residues within those domains that are important for that function (El-Gebali et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes the intended purpose of the FAIDR method.

claim: Homologs of the N-terminal IDR of Mfg1 show elevated variance in glutamine repeats.
source: The analysis of Mfg1 also reveals that homologs of the N-terminal IDR show elevated variance in glutamine repeats, a property of IDRs that we find associated with transcription factor function, consistent with previous reports (Freiman and Tjian, 2002; Gemayel et al., 2015; Klemsz and Maki, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 5C and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Elevated variance in glutamine repeats is associated with transcription factor function.
source: The analysis of Mfg1 also reveals that homologs of the N-terminal IDR show elevated variance in glutamine repeats, a property of IDRs that we find associated with transcription factor function, consistent with previous reports (Freiman and Tjian, 2002; Gemayel et al., 2015; Klemsz and Maki, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by FAIDR analysis and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Modulation of the glutamine residues in the N-terminal IDR of Mfg1 will impact its function in transcription.
source: Thus, we can formulate the hypothesis that this specific sequence feature is important for function, and test this by modulating the number of glutamine repeats in the lab (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is presented as a testable hypothesis based on FAIDR predictions.

claim: Molecular features based on single sequences did not perform as well as evolutionary features.
source: While FAIDR analysis using descriptions of molecular features based on single sequences would be easier to interpret, we found that our features did not perform as well when computed on S. cerevisiae alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In addition to previously reported molecular features, FAIDR found an unexpected depletion of threonine residues in IDRs in most classes of RNA-binding proteins.
source: In addition to other previously reported molecular features (the expected short linear motifs and repeats associated with signaling, posttranslational regulation, and RNA binding), we found an unexpected depletion of threonine residues in IDRs in most classes of RNA-binding proteins
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B and is stated as a novel finding.

claim: FAIDR found an unexpected decreased variance of lysine residues specific to stress-granule proteins.
source: and an unexpected decreased variance of lysine residues specific to stress-granule proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the feature analysis shown in Figure 3B and is stated as a novel finding.

claim: Hydrophobicity and isoelectric point are not the only two features that are important for mitochondrial localization.
source: We note that hydrophobicity and isoelectric point are only two of the top features that we chose to focus on in this study and are not the only two features that are important for mitochondrial localization.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of mitochondrial targeting signals and the authors' interpretation of their results.

claim: Features including positive charge, potential to form an amphipathic helix, hydrophobicity, and the presence of cleavage motifs can help identify mitochondrial targeting signals.
source: It is known that features including positive charge, potential to form an amphipathic helix, hydrophobicity, and the presence of cleavage motifs can help identify mitochondrial targeting signals (Fukasawa et al., 2015; Garg and Gould, 2016; Roise and Schatz, 1988; Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on mitochondrial targeting signals.

claim: Mitochondrial pre-sequences are known to form helices upon interacting with their target receptor.
source: Furthermore, while mitochondrial pre-sequences are known to form helices upon interacting with their target receptor, they do not engage in a stable interaction and sample different conformations (Abe et al., 2000; Kohda, 2018; Saitoh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on mitochondrial pre-sequences.

claim: Mitochondrial pre-sequences do not engage in a stable interaction and sample different conformations.
source: Furthermore, while mitochondrial pre-sequences are known to form helices upon interacting with their target receptor, they do not engage in a stable interaction and sample different conformations (Abe et al., 2000; Kohda, 2018; Saitoh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on mitochondrial pre-sequences.

claim: Artificially increasing the isoelectric point of a simulated Cox15 N-terminal IDR enabled creation of a weak synthetic targeting signal.
source: Remarkably, we also found that artificially increasing the isoelectric point of a simulated Cox15 N-terminal IDR (i.e., an IDR with no enrichment of sequence-distributed features) enabled us to create a weak synthetic targeting signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The synthetic mitochondrial targeting signal created by increasing pI in a simulated Cox15 IDR represents the first synthetic IDR designed to perform a specific biological function.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first synthetic IDR designed to perform a specific biological function
evidence: The claim is stated as a novel achievement based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Eight amino acid changes were sufficient to create a weak synthetic mitochondrial targeting signal.
source: we could hand-design mutations in a synthetic IDR to perform a desired function through eight amino acid changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Diverse functions can be associated with the IDR sequence features included in evolutionary signatures.
source: In all, we found that diverse functions can be associated with the IDR sequence features included in our evolutionary signatures (Zarin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by the predictive performance results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The features of disordered regions used in evolutionary signatures were obtained from a review of the literature.
source: However, we note that these features of disordered regions were obtained from a review of the literature, and new features are continuously being discovered (e.g., patterning of aromatic residues [Martin et al., 2020]).
evidence: The claim describes the source of the molecular features used in the study.

claim: Including newly discovered features will likely further improve predictive power of FAIDR.
source: It is likely that including these features will further improve predictive power of the approach described here.
evidence: The claim is speculation about future improvements to the method.

claim: FAIDR uses protein-level functional annotations from the Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD).
source: We trained FAIDR models using protein-level functional annotations from the Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD) (Cherry et al., 2012) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the data source used for training FAIDR.

claim: FAIDR uses evolutionary signatures calculated for IDRs predicted from the S. cerevisiae proteome using DISOPRED3 that are 30 amino acids or longer.
source: In order to calculate evolutionary signatures from predicted IDRs (disordered regions predicted from the S. cerevisiae proteome using DISOPRED3 [Jones and Cozzetto, 2015] that are 30 amino acids or longer)
evidence: The claim describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: For each set of orthologous IDRs, 1000 sets of orthologous IDRs were simulated using previously described methods.
source: Briefly, for each set of orthologous IDRs (obtained from the Yeast Gene Order Browser [Byrne and Wolfe, 2005] and filtered to include those proteins for which there are 10 or more orthologs), we simulated 1000 sets of orthologous IDRs using previously described methods (Nguyen Ba et al., 2014; Nguyen Ba et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: A negative Z-score in evolutionary signatures implies that the evolution (in mean or variance) of a molecular feature is lower than the null expectation.
source: A negative Z-score implies that the evolution (in mean or variance) of a molecular feature is lower than our null expectation, while a positive Z-score implies that the evolution (in mean or variance) of a molecular feature is higher than our null expectation for the given IDR.
evidence: The claim describes the interpretation of evolutionary signatures.

claim: A positive Z-score in evolutionary signatures implies that the evolution (in mean or variance) of a molecular feature is higher than the null expectation.
source: A negative Z-score implies that the evolution (in mean or variance) of a molecular feature is lower than our null expectation, while a positive Z-score implies that the evolution (in mean or variance) of a molecular feature is higher than our null expectation for the given IDR.
evidence: The claim describes the interpretation of evolutionary signatures.

claim: A Z-score around zero in evolutionary signatures implies that the molecular feature is evolving according to the null expectation of IDR evolution.
source: A Z-score around zero implies that the molecular feature in question is evolving according to our null expectation of IDR evolution.
evidence: The claim describes the interpretation of evolutionary signatures.

claim: The null expectation for IDR evolution includes selection to preserve amino acid residue frequency according to disordered region-specific substitution matrices, but no selection to preserve the sequence-distributed molecular features.
source: The null expectation includes selection to preserve amino acid residue frequency according to disordered region-specific substitution matrices, but no selection to preserve the sequence-distributed molecular features.
evidence: The claim describes the null model used in calculating evolutionary signatures.

claim: Mitochondrial targeting signals were obtained from a global analysis that identified and validated mitochondrial targeting signals in highly purified mitochondria using combined fractional diagonal chromatography.
source: First, we obtained a dataset of mitochondrial targeting signals from a global analysis that identified and validated mitochondrial targeting signals in highly purified mitochondria using combined fractional diagonal chromatography (Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim describes the source of the mitochondrial targeting signal data used for validation.

claim: Cdc28 phosphorylation sites were obtained from high-throughput kinase-specific mass spectrometry experiments.
source: Second, we obtained Cdc28 phosphorylation sites discovered in high-throughput kinase-specific mass spectrometry experiments (Holt et al., 2009; Lai et al., 2012) and mapped them to IDRs.
evidence: The claim describes the source of the Cdc28 substrate data used for validation.

claim: Out of 1016 IDRs in the test set, 49 (5%) had sequence similarity to IDRs in the training set (BLAST e-value less than 10−5).
source: We found that out of 1016 IDRs in the test set, 49 (5%) had sequence similarity to IDRs in the training set (i.e., had a BLAST e-value that was less than 10−5).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST analysis performed to check for circularity between training and test sets.

claim: For mitochondrial targeting signals, sequence similarity explains at most 3% of FAIDR's predictive power.
source: For mitochondrial targeting signals, this sequence similarity explains at most 3% of our predictive power (1/35 IDRs in the positive test set have sequence similarity to IDRs in the training set according to the above e-value threshold).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of sequence similarity between training and test sets.

claim: For CDK targets, sequence similarity explains at most 10% of FAIDR's predictive power.
source: For CDK targets, this sequence similarity explains at most 10% of our predictive power (6/59 IDRs in the positive test set have sequence similarity to IDRs in the training set according to the above e-value threshold).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of sequence similarity between training and test sets.

claim: IDRs with sequence similarity tend to be in paralogous proteins.
source: IDRs with sequence similarity tend to be in paralogous proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the proteins containing IDRs with sequence similarity.

claim: FAIDR was implemented in R with the glmnet package.
source: FAIDR was implemented in R with the glmnet package (Friedman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim describes the implementation of the FAIDR method.

claim: FAIDR code and results are available at https://github.com/taraneh-z/FAIDR.
source: Code and results are available at https://github.com/taraneh-z/FAIDR; Zarin, 2021; copy archived at swh:1:rev:b1ef30705f7133f21201166522077a062984566b.
evidence: The claim provides information about data and code availability.

claim: Evolutionary signatures are available for download and visualization at http://www.moseslab.csb.utoronto.ca/idr/.
source: Evolutionary signatures are available for download and visualization at http://www.moseslab.csb.utoronto.ca/idr/.
evidence: The claim provides information about data availability.

claim: Confocal microscopy was used to image Cox15-GFP strains using a Leica TCS-SP8 with 63× oil immersion objective.
source: Confocal microscopy (Leica TCS-SP8, 63× oil immersion objective, Leica HyD hybrid detectors) was used to image cells.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Cells were treated with 0.5 µg/ml DAPI in SD-complete growth media for 15 min for mitochondrial DNA staining.
source: Where applicable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), cells were treated with 0.5 µg/ml DAPI in SD-complete growth media for 15 min.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used.

claim: To improve numerical stability of IRLS, a small L2 penalty (alpha = 0.99 in glmnet) was used.
source: To improve the numerical stability of IRLS (needed when we had small numbers of positive examples relative to the number of features), we also used a small L2 penalty (alpha = 0.99 in glmnet)
evidence: The claim describes a parameter choice in the FAIDR implementation.
